---
title: "Validation Against Published Results"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)

# The cache is in the repository beside the script that makes it. The path is
# relative to this article, which is where knitr and pkgdown evaluate it.
cache <- file.path("..", "..", "data-raw", "validation_results.rds")
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  stop("This article displays data-raw/validation_results.rds, which was not found. ",
       "Render it from a copy of the repository.", call. = FALSE)
}
res <- readRDS(cache)
if (!isTRUE(attr(res, "scale") == 1) || !identical(attr(res, "only"), "")) {
  stop("The cached results are from a trial run. Run data-raw/validation_study.R ",
       "at full size and for every condition.", call. = FALSE)
}

num <- function(x, d = 2) {
  out <- formatC(round(x, d) + 0, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
  out[is.na(x)] <- ""
  out
}
int <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
with_se <- function(x, se, d) ifelse(is.na(se), num(x, d), sprintf("%s (%s)", num(x, d), num(se, d)))

# Rows of one family, optionally narrowed by exact kind and by a pattern in
# the procedure, the condition, the source, or the quantity.
rows <- function(family, kind = NULL, procedure = NULL, condition = NULL,
                 source = NULL, quantity = NULL) {
  x <- res[res$family == family, ]
  if (!is.null(kind)) x <- x[x$kind %in% kind, ]
  if (!is.null(procedure)) x <- x[grepl(procedure, x$procedure, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (!is.null(condition)) x <- x[grepl(condition, x$condition, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (!is.null(source)) x <- x[grepl(source, x$source, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (!is.null(quantity)) x <- x[grepl(quantity, x$quantity, fixed = TRUE), ]
  x
}
# Exactly one row, or an error: every number quoted in the text is found by name.
one <- function(...) {
  x <- rows(...)
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one row, found ", nrow(x), call. = FALSE)
  x
}

# One line per condition for an interval procedure: mean final sample size,
# coverage, and mean width, each beside the published value. `who` names the
# source of the simulated value: the package, or, where a rule as printed is
# simulated, "simulated".
interval_table <- function(x, n_digits = 1, label = "Condition", who = "package") {
  key <- unique(paste(x$procedure, x$condition, sep = " | "))
  id <- paste(x$procedure, x$condition, sep = " | ")
  part <- function(quantity) x[x$quantity == quantity, ][match(key, id[x$quantity == quantity]), ]
  n <- part("mean final sample size"); p <- part("coverage"); w <- part("mean interval width")
  out <- data.frame(
    n$condition, int(n$replications),
    num(n$published, n_digits), with_se(n$value, n$se, n_digits), num(n$z, 1),
    num(p$published, 4), with_se(p$value, p$se, 4), num(p$z, 1),
    num(w$published, 4), num(w$value, 4), num(w$z, 1))
  knitr::kable(out, align = c("l", rep("r", 10)),
               col.names = c(label, "Replications", "N, article",
                             sprintf("N, %s (SE)", who), "z", "Coverage, article",
                             sprintf("Coverage, %s (SE)", who), "z", "Width, article",
                             sprintf("Width, %s", who), "z"))
}
# One line per row: the quantity, the reference value, the package's value.
long_table <- function(x, digits = 4, reference = "Published", first = "condition",
                       first_label = "Condition", show_quantity = TRUE, show_n = FALSE,
                       quantity_label = "Quantity", value_label = "Package (SE)") {
  d <- rep_len(digits, nrow(x))
  out <- data.frame(x[[first]])
  names <- first_label
  if (show_quantity) { out <- cbind(out, x$quantity); names <- c(names, quantity_label) }
  out <- cbind(out, mapply(num, x$published, d),
               mapply(function(v, s, k) with_se(v, s, k), x$value, x$se, d),
               ifelse(is.na(x$replications), "", int(x$replications)), num(x$z, 1))
  names <- c(names, reference, value_label, "Replications", "z")
  if (show_n) { out <- cbind(out, num(x$mean_n, 1)); names <- c(names, "Mean N") }
  knitr::kable(out, align = c(rep("l", ncol(out) - 4L - show_n), rep("r", 4L + show_n)),
               col.names = names)
}
within <- function(x, limit = 2) sum(abs(x$z) <= limit, na.rm = TRUE)
largest <- function(x) num(max(abs(x$z), na.rm = TRUE), 1)
# The standard deviation over studies behind a mean and its standard error:
# found here, and implied by the standard error of the published mean.
sd_here <- function(x) x$se * sqrt(x$replications)
sd_published <- function(x, replications = 5000) x$published_se * sqrt(replications)
# A list in a sentence: "a, b, and c".
listing <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 3L) paste(x, collapse = " and ")
  else paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), ", and ", x[length(x)])
}
# Words for a small count.
count_word <- function(n) if (n == 0) "none" else if (n <= 10) c("one", "two", "three", "four",
  "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[n] else as.character(n)
# The comparisons of a simulated value from the package with a published
# simulation value, a population value, or an exact value.
compared <- res[res$kind %in% c("published simulation", "population value", "exact calculation",
                                "exact calculation, second run") &
                  !is.na(res$se) & !is.na(res$z), ]
```

Every sequential procedure in SMSD comes from a published source, and most
of those sources report what the procedure does: a simulation table, a worked
example, or a result that can be computed exactly. This article sets the
package beside those reports. It shows where the package reproduces them,
where it does not, where it differs on purpose and why, and, at the end, what
the procedures do not deliver when the target is wide.

Nothing is simulated when this page is built. The numbers come from one
script, `data-raw/validation_study.R` in the package's repository, which runs
each procedure through the package's exported functions and saves the results.
The page reads that file:

```{r load, echo = TRUE}
results <- readRDS(file.path("..", "..", "data-raw", "validation_results.rds"))
dim(results)
names(results)
c(date = attr(results, "date"), SMSD = attr(results, "package_version"),
  seed = attr(results, "seed"))
```

The study took `r num(attr(res, "minutes") + attr(res, "second_run_minutes"), 0)`
minutes on `r attr(res, "cores")` cores
(`r num(attr(res, "processor_minutes") + attr(res, "second_run_processor_minutes"), 0)`
minutes of processor time). Each simulated condition was run in
`r attr(res, "parts")` parts with their own seeds, so the results do not
depend on the number of cores, and the script can be run again to check them
(see the last section).

## How to Read the Tables

Each table sets a value from a source beside the value the package gives for
the same condition.

- **The package's value** comes from the exported functions only. Where a
  `*_sensitivity()` function generates the article's data, that function ran
  the procedure. Otherwise the pilot function and the check function were
  called in the loop a study would run: start at the pilot sample size, add
  one observation, check, and stop the first time the check reports the
  stopping rule as met.
- **SE** is the Monte Carlo standard error of the package's value.
- **z** is the package's value minus the published value, divided by the
  standard error of that difference. The standard error combines three
  things: the Monte Carlo error of the package's value, the Monte Carlo error
  of the published value where that value is itself a simulation mean, and
  the rounding of the published value to the decimals printed. For the
  Monte Carlo error of a published mean the study uses the standard error
  that the article prints. Where an article prints none (the mean widths of
  the 2018 tables and of the squared multiple correlation tables, for
  example), it uses the standard error that the spread found in this study
  gives a mean of the article's 5,000 replications. A value of z between -2
  and 2 is what chance alone
  produces 95 times in 100. With several thousand replications on each side
  the comparison is sharp: a z of 5 can belong to a difference in the fourth
  decimal.
- **Replications** is the number of simulated studies behind the package's
  value. It is empty where the value is not simulated.
- **N** is the final sample size: the number of observations at which the
  procedure stopped.

The reproduction sections below hold `r nrow(compared)` comparisons of a
simulated value from the package with a published simulation value, a
population value, or an exact value, so a few values of z beyond 2 are
expected by chance alone even where the package and the source agree exactly.
(The cached file has `r nrow(res)` rows in all. The others are worked examples
and closed forms, which have no sampling error; rows in which the package
departs from its source on purpose, or in which a rule as printed is
simulated in place of the package's; and rows set beside a nominal level or a
bound and not beside a published value, most of them in the last section.)
Where the reference value is exact, a difference of more than
three standard errors can only be chance or a defect, and the study settles
which by running that condition a second time, with new seeds and ten times
the replications; both runs are shown. A row that does not reproduce is shown
as it is.

## A Narrow Confidence Interval: Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018)

```{r aipe-2018}
a18 <- rows("aipe_2018")
smd18 <- one("aipe_2018", condition = "means 10 and 9.5", quantity = "mean final sample size")
sd18 <- smd18$published_se * sqrt(5000)
```

Tables 2 to 4 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, pp. 233--234) report
the mean final sample size, the coverage, and the mean width of the interval
for the standardized mean difference (95% intervals no wider than 0.2) and for
the coefficient of variation (90% and 95% intervals no wider than 0.04). The
rows below are the two normal conditions of Table 2 with standardized mean
differences of 0.3 and 0.5, and the normal, gamma, and lognormal populations
with a coefficient of variation of 0.2 from Tables 3 and 4. For the standardized
mean difference the sample size is per group.

```{r aipe-2018-table}
interval_table(a18)
```

Of the `r nrow(a18)` comparisons, `r within(a18)` are within two standard
errors and the largest difference is `r largest(a18)` standard errors. The
package reproduces these tables.

One detail of the comparison needs a note. The article's tables print a column
s(N) described as the standard error of the mean final sample size, and its
entries are far too small to be that. For the standardized mean difference of
0.5 the entry is 0.0026, while the standard deviation of the final sample size
in this study is `r num(sd18, 1)`, which gives a mean of 5,000 replications a
standard error of `r num(smd18$published_se, 2)`. (The printed entry is close
to that standard deviation divided by 5,000.) The standard error of each
published mean final sample size in this section is therefore computed from
the standard deviation found here and the article's 5,000 replications. The
tables print no standard error for the mean width, so its standard error is
computed in the same way.

## Correlation Coefficients: Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019)

```{r corr-2019}
c19 <- rows("correlations_2019")
pear <- rows("correlations_2019", procedure = "Pearson")
kend <- rows("correlations_2019", procedure = "Kendall")
spear <- rows("correlations_2019", procedure = "Spearman")
k5 <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Kendall", condition = "rho = 0.5",
          quantity = "mean final sample size")
k1 <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Kendall", condition = "rho = 0.1",
          quantity = "mean final sample size")
k5c <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Kendall", condition = "rho = 0.5",
           quantity = "coverage")
k1c <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Kendall", condition = "rho = 0.1",
           quantity = "coverage")
p5 <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Pearson", condition = "rho = 0.5; width 0.2",
          quantity = "mean final sample size")
p5c <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Pearson", condition = "rho = 0.5; width 0.2",
           quantity = "coverage")
p5w <- one("correlations_2019", procedure = "Pearson", condition = "rho = 0.5; width 0.2",
           quantity = "mean interval width")
kn <- rbind(k5, k1)
kw <- kend[kend$quantity == "mean interval width", ]
# z for the Kendall means with the spread found here, in place of the
# article's standard error, behind the article's 5,000 replications.
z_own <- function(x) {
  (x$value - x$published) /
    sqrt(x$se^2 + sd_here(x)^2 / 5000 + (10^-x$published_digits)^2 / 12)
}
```

The rows are from Table 2 (Pearson, p. 498), Table 8 (Kendall, p. 502), and
Table 10 (Spearman, p. 503) of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019):
bivariate normal data and 95% intervals. The Pearson rows were run by
`seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()`; that function studies the Pearson correlation
only, so the Kendall and Spearman rows were run through `seq_aipe_r_pilot()`
and `seq_aipe_r()`. The coverage of a rank correlation is counted against its
own population value (0.3333 for Kendall and 0.4826 for Spearman when &rho; =
0.5, as the article gives them).

```{r corr-2019-table}
c19_show <- c19
c19_show$condition <- sprintf("%s, %s", sub("^.*, ", "", c19$procedure),
                              sub("^bivariate normal, (.*), 95%$", "\\1", c19$condition))
interval_table(c19_show)
```

**Pearson.** The mean final sample sizes are within
`r largest(pear[pear$quantity == "mean final sample size", ])` standard errors
of the article's. At &rho; = 0.5 and a width of 0.2 the package's studies run
slightly longer, cover slightly more often, and end with slightly wider
intervals than the article's (`r num(p5$value, 1)` against
`r num(p5$published, 1)` pairs, coverage `r num(p5c$value, 3)` against
`r num(p5c$published, 3)`, mean width `r num(p5w$value, 4)` against
`r num(p5w$published, 4)`, the last a difference of `r num(p5w$z, 1)`
standard errors). All three are the effect of a deliberate departure
described below: the package does not stop on a variance estimate that is
zero or negative. Coverage of about 0.90 at a
nominal 0.95 in that row is the article's own finding, and the package's too.
It is taken up in the last section.

**Kendall.** The mean final sample sizes and mean widths of these rows do not
reproduce. The package's mean final sample size is `r num(k5$value, 1)`
against the article's
`r num(k5$published, 1)` at &rho; = 0.5 and `r num(k1$value, 1)` against
`r num(k1$published, 1)` at &rho; = 0.1, differences of `r num(k5$z, 0)` and
`r num(k1$z, 0)` standard errors. The final sample size also varies far more
from study to study than the article's standard errors imply: its standard
deviation is `r num(sd_here(k5), 1)` here against `r num(sd_published(k5), 1)`
at &rho; = 0.5, about `r num(sd_here(k5) / sd_published(k5), 0)` times as
large, and `r num(sd_here(k1), 1)` against `r num(sd_published(k1), 1)` at
&rho; = 0.1, about `r num(sd_here(k1) / sd_published(k1), 0)` times as large.
(With the spread found here in place of the article's standard errors, the
two means are still `r num(z_own(k5), 0)` and `r num(z_own(k1), 0)` standard
errors from the article's.) The differences in the means are small in
practical terms, about
`r num(100 * max(kn$value / kn$published - 1), 0)` percent of the sample size
and at most `r num(max(abs(kw$value - kw$published)), 4)` in mean width, but
they are far outside Monte Carlo error. Coverage does agree with the
article's: `r num(k5c$value, 3)` against `r num(k5c$published, 3)` at
&rho; = 0.5 and `r num(k1c$value, 3)` against `r num(k1c$published, 3)` at
&rho; = 0.1, differences of `r num(k5c$z, 1)` and `r num(k1c$z, 1)` standard
errors. The package
computes the variance estimator of the article's Equations 27 to 29
(p. 500); its tests compare the code with a transcription of those equations
and with the large sample value for bivariate normal data. The cause is
therefore most likely a difference between the printed equations and the
code behind the article's table, and it cannot be settled without that code.

**Spearman.** The row is reproduced within
`r largest(spear)` standard errors.

## The Squared Multiple Correlation: Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019)

```{r r2-2019}
r2 <- rows("r2_2019")
r2n <- r2[r2$quantity == "mean final sample size", ]
r2p <- r2[r2$quantity == "coverage", ]
r2w <- r2[r2$quantity == "mean interval width", ]
low <- r2p[which.min(r2p$published), ]
far <- r2n[abs(r2n$z) > 3, ]
r2_far <- if (nrow(far) == 0L) "" else sprintf(
  "The %s by more than three standard errors %s within %s observations (%s percent) of the article's.",
  if (nrow(far) == 1L) "one mean that differs" else paste(nrow(far), "means that differ"),
  if (nrow(far) == 1L) "is" else "are",
  num(max(abs(far$value - far$published)), 1),
  num(100 * max(abs(far$value / far$published - 1)), 1))
r2w_far <- if (sum(abs(r2w$z) > 3) == 0L) {
  sprintf("none is more than three (the largest is %s)", largest(r2w))
} else {
  sprintf("%s more than three (the largest is %s)",
          if (sum(abs(r2w$z) > 3) == 1L) "one is" else paste(count_word(sum(abs(r2w$z) > 3)), "are"),
          largest(r2w))
}
```

Tables 11 to 14 of the same article (pp. 504--507) cover the squared multiple
correlation with multivariate normal data: the log transformed interval at 90%
(Table 11) and 95% (Table 12), and the Wald interval at 90% (Table 13) and 95%
(Table 14). The rows below are those with a target width of 0.10, 2 and 5
predictors, and population values of 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9, run by
`seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity()`.

```{r r2-2019-table}
r2_show <- r2
r2_show$condition <- sprintf("Table %s: %s", sub("^.*Table ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", r2$source),
                             sub("; width 0.10", "", r2$condition, fixed = TRUE))
interval_table(r2_show, n_digits = 2)
```

Of the `r nrow(r2n)` mean final sample sizes, `r within(r2n)` are within two
standard errors of the article's and `r within(r2n, 3)` within three (the
largest difference is `r largest(r2n)`); of the `r nrow(r2p)` coverages,
`r within(r2p)` are within two and `r within(r2p, 3)` within three (largest
`r largest(r2p)`). `r r2_far` The mean widths agree with the article's within
`r num(max(abs(r2w$value - r2w$published)), 4)` in every row: of the
`r nrow(r2w)` differences, `r within(r2w)` are within two standard errors and
`r r2w_far`. (The tables print no standard error for the mean width; the one
used is described under How to Read the Tables.)
The low coverages in these tables are the
article's as well as the package's: `r num(low$published, 3)` in the article
and `r num(low$value, 3)` here for the `r sub(";.*$", "", low$condition)` row of
the `r sub("^seq_aipe_R2\\(\\), ", "", low$procedure)` at
`r sub("^.*, ", "", low$condition)`. The Wald
rows are reproduced by a stopping rule that differs in one sign from the
article's Equation 63 as printed; see the departures below.

## Minimum Risk for the Coefficient of Variation: Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016)

```{r mr-cv}
m16 <- rows("mrpe_cv_2016")
pub16 <- rows("mrpe_cv_2016", kind = "published simulation")
ex16 <- rows("mrpe_cv_2016", kind = "worked example")
```

Table 1 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, p. 642) gives the mean final sample
size of the minimum risk procedure for populations with coefficients of
variation from 0.2 to 0.8 (A = 5,000,000 and c = 10). The article's procedure
estimates the variance of the sample coefficient of variation with its
Equation 22, which `seq_mr_cv()` offers as `variance = "published"`. With that
option the package reproduces the eight rows below:

```{r mr-cv-table}
pub16_show <- pub16
pub16_show$condition <- sub("; A = .*$", "", pub16$condition)
long_table(pub16_show, digits = 2, reference = "Article", first_label = "Population",
           show_quantity = FALSE)
```

All `r nrow(pub16)` are within `r largest(pub16)` standard errors. The
default of `seq_mr_cv()` is a different variance, and gives different sample
sizes for populations that are not normal; that departure has its own section
below.

The article's worked example (p. 638) prints the output of its function for 35
observations with A = 400,000 and c = 75:

```{r mr-cv-example}
ex16$agree <- abs(ex16$value - ex16$published) <= 0.5 * 10^-ex16$published_digits * (1 + 1e-8)
knitr::kable(data.frame(ex16$condition, ex16$quantity,
                        mapply(num, ex16$published, ex16$published_digits),
                        mapply(num, ex16$value, ex16$published_digits),
                        ifelse(ex16$agree, "yes", "no")),
             align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "l"),
             col.names = c("Data", "Quantity", "Article", "Package", "Same to the digits printed"))
```

`r if (all(ex16$agree)) "Every printed value is reproduced, and" else "Not every printed value is reproduced;"`
`seq_path()` finds the rule first met at
`r int(one("mrpe_cv_2016", quantity = "first sample size")$value)` observations,
as the article reports.

## Minimum Risk for the Standardized Mean Difference: Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017)

```{r mr-smd}
m17 <- rows("mrpe_smd_2017", kind = "published simulation")
ex17 <- one("mrpe_smd_2017", kind = "worked example")
```

Tables 1 and 3 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, pp. 103--104) give the mean
final sample size per group of the equal cost procedure for two normal
populations, at two settings of the loss constant and the cost. They were run
by `seq_mr_smd_sensitivity()`.

```{r mr-smd-table}
m17_show <- m17
m17_show$condition <- sprintf("%s: %s", sub("^.*(Table [0-9]+).*$", "\\1", m17$source),
                              m17$condition)
long_table(m17_show, digits = 4, reference = "Article", show_quantity = FALSE)
```

Of the `r nrow(m17)` means, `r within(m17)` are within two standard errors of
the article's (largest difference `r largest(m17)`). In the worked example of
p. 106 (a sample standardized mean difference of 1.00, A = 10,000, c = 2.40)
the article reports that the rule is met at 75 per group and at no smaller
sample size; `seq_mr_smd()` first reports it met at
`r int(ex17$value)`. The article has no simulation table for its procedure
with two different costs; the script `data-raw/smd_mrpe_simulation.R` in the
repository checks that procedure against the sample sizes that minimize the
article's risk function.

## A Contrast Under a Budget: Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025)

```{r budget}
closed <- rows("budget_2025", kind = "closed form")
closed$agree <- abs(closed$value - closed$published) <=
  0.5 * 10^-closed$published_digits * (1 + 1e-8)
miss <- closed[!closed$agree, ]
stopifnot(nrow(miss) == 1L, grepl("mixture", miss$condition),
          grepl("minimum variance", miss$quantity))
fp <- rows("budget_2025", procedure = "first_passage")
re <- rows("budget_2025", procedure = "reallocate")
lit <- rows("budget_2025", kind = "rule as printed")
part_of <- function(x, quantity) {
  y <- x[grepl(quantity, x$quantity, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(y) != 1L) stop("Expected one row for: ", quantity, call. = FALSE)
  y
}
fp_n <- fp[grepl("mean final sample size", fp$quantity), ]
lit_n <- lit[grepl("mean final sample size", lit$quantity), ]
fp_v <- part_of(fp, "estimated variance"); lit_v <- part_of(lit, "estimated variance")
fp_c <- part_of(fp, "mean total cost"); re_c <- part_of(re, "mean total cost")
lit_c <- part_of(lit, "mean total cost")
fp_both <- rbind(fp_n, fp_v); lit_both <- rbind(lit_n, lit_v)
v_opt <- one("budget_2025", kind = "closed form", condition = "normal populations",
             quantity = "minimum variance")
fp_within <- part_of(fp, "within the budget"); re_within <- part_of(re, "within the budget")
# The sentences below state these; a cache that no longer supports them stops the build.
stopifnot(nrow(fp_n) == 3L, nrow(lit_n) == 3L, all(abs(fp_n$z[1:2]) < 2), fp_n$z[3] > 2,
          abs(fp_v$z) > 3, abs(lit_v$z) > 3, max(abs(lit_n$z)) > 3,
          max(abs(lit_n$z)) >= max(abs(fp_n$z)), abs(lit_c$z) < 2)
```

**Optimal allocation.** `seq_budget_optimal()` gives the sample sizes and the
variance that the article derives for known standard deviations. The example
of p. 430 (three groups, 30 per observation, a budget of 10,000) and the
optimal sample sizes and minimum variances of all four blocks of Table 1
(p. 431; a budget of 5,000 and weights 1, -2, 1) make
`r nrow(closed)` printed values, and the package agrees with
`r sum(closed$agree)` of them to the last digit printed:

```{r budget-closed}
knitr::kable(data.frame(sub("; budget.*$", "", closed$condition), closed$quantity,
                        mapply(num, closed$published, closed$published_digits),
                        mapply(num, closed$value, closed$published_digits),
                        ifelse(closed$agree, "yes", "no")),
             align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "l"),
             col.names = c("Design", "Quantity", "Article", "Package", "Same to the digits printed"))
```

The one exception is the minimum variance of the mixture block, printed as
`r num(miss$published, 4)`. The article's own formula gives
`r num(miss$value, 4)` for the standard deviations that reproduce that
block's three sample sizes, so the printed value appears to be a misprint.

**The sequential procedure.** For the normal block of Table 1 the article
reports the mean final sample size of each group and the mean of the estimated
variance over 5,000 studies with a pilot sample of 10 per group (p. 432).
`seq_budget_sensitivity()` ran the same design under both of the package's
procedures. `procedure = "first_passage"` is the package's reading of the
article's rule, in which a group is closed for good the first time it meets
its criterion; `procedure = "reallocate"`, the default, judges every group on
the current data at every step. The first passage option is not a step for
step copy of the article's sequence (the help page of `seq_budget_next()`
lists three differences), so the study also ran that sequence itself, written
out step for step from pp. 429--430 of the article in base R with no package
code. It is the third block of the table.

```{r budget-sim}
both <- rbind(fp, re, lit)
both <- both[both$kind != "nominal level", ]
both$condition <- ifelse(grepl("first_passage", both$procedure), "`first_passage`",
                         ifelse(grepl("reallocate", both$procedure), "`reallocate`",
                                "Article's sequence, step for step"))
long_table(both, reference = "Article", first_label = "Procedure",
           value_label = "Simulated (SE)",
           digits = ifelse(grepl("percent", both$quantity), 0,
                           ifelse(grepl("variance", both$quantity), 4,
                                  ifelse(grepl("cost", both$quantity), 1, 3))))
```

The article's table prints no mean cost. The value in the "Article" column
of those rows is the cost its mean final sample sizes imply: the sum over the
groups of the cost of an observation (38, 15, and 10) times the mean final
sample size. For the estimated variance the table prints a mean absolute
deviation (0.0285) and no standard error; z uses a standard error
for the article's mean taken from it by the relation that holds for a normal
variable.

The table is reproduced only in part, and the article's own sequence does
not reproduce it either. With the first passage rule the mean final sample
sizes of the first two groups agree with the article's
(`r num(fp_n$z[1], 1)` and `r num(fp_n$z[2], 1)` standard errors) and that of
the third is higher (`r num(fp_n$value[3], 2)` against
`r num(fp_n$published[3], 2)`, `r num(fp_n$z[3], 1)` standard errors); the
mean of the estimated variance is `r num(fp_v$value, 4)` where the article
reports `r num(fp_v$published, 4)` (`r num(fp_v$z, 1)` standard errors); the
smallest attainable variance for this design is `r num(v_opt$value, 4)`. The
article's sequence, step for step, is no closer: its mean final sample sizes
are `r listing(num(lit_n$z, 1))` standard errors from the table's, and its
mean estimated variance is `r num(lit_v$value, 4)`
(`r num(lit_v$z, 1)`). The differences are small, at most
`r num(100 * max(abs(fp_both$value / fp_both$published - 1)), 1)` percent for
the first passage option and
`r num(100 * max(abs(lit_both$value / lit_both$published - 1)), 1)` percent
for the article's sequence, but the largest are outside Monte Carlo error
under both, so the package's reading of the sequence is not what separates
it from the table. What does could not be determined from the article. The
cost that the table implies is reproduced by the article's sequence, which
spent `r num(lit_c$value, 1)` of the 5,000 on average against the implied
`r num(lit_c$published, 1)` (`r num(lit_c$z, 1)` standard errors). The first
passage option spent `r num(fp_c$value, 1)` (`r num(fp_c$z, 1)`), and the
default `r num(re_c$value, 1)`.

What the article claims for the procedure does hold: no study exceeded the
budget (`r num(fp_within$value, 0)` percent within it under the first passage
rule and `r num(re_within$value, 0)` under the default), and the coverage of
the 95% interval was
`r num(one("budget_2025", procedure = "first_passage", quantity = "coverage")$value, 3)`
and `r num(one("budget_2025", procedure = "reallocate", quantity = "coverage")$value, 3)`.
The default is the package's choice and not the article's procedure; the
help page of `seq_budget()` gives the reasons.

## The Gini Index: Chattopadhyay and De (2016)

```{r gini}
g_pop <- rows("gini_2016", kind = "population value")
g_sim <- rows("gini_2016", procedure = "seq_aipe_gini_pilot")
g_row <- function(population, quantity) {
  x <- g_sim[grepl(paste0("^", population), g_sim$condition) &
               grepl(quantity, g_sim$quantity, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one row for: ", population, call. = FALSE)
  x
}
populations <- c("gamma", "lognormal", "Pareto")
g_n <- do.call(rbind, lapply(populations, g_row, "mean final sample size"))
g_art <- do.call(rbind, lapply(populations, g_row, "the article's interval"))
g_pkg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(populations, g_row, "the package reports"))
gam_n <- g_n[1, ]; log_n <- g_n[2, ]; par_n <- g_n[3, ]
# The smallest and largest final sample sizes found here, and the largest in
# the posted version, from the note of the row.
range_of <- function(x) as.numeric(regmatches(x$note, gregexpr("[0-9]+", x$note))[[1]])
gam_range <- range_of(gam_n)
# The sentences below state these; a cache that no longer supports them stops the build.
stopifnot(length(gam_range) == 3L, nrow(g_pop) == 6L, nrow(g_sim) == 9L,
          abs(log_n$z) < 2, abs(par_n$z) < 2, abs(gam_n$z) > 3)
# The optimal fixed sample size of the article (the smallest n that is at
# least z^2 xi^2 / d^2) at a half width of 0.01 and 90%, from the population
# variances, in the order gamma, lognormal, Pareto.
g_xi2 <- g_pop$published[grepl("variance", g_pop$quantity)]
g_fixed <- floor(qnorm(0.95)^2 * g_xi2 / 0.01^2) + 1
# The mean width of the interval the package reports, from the note of the row.
g_width <- as.numeric(sub("^mean width ([0-9.]+),.*$", "\\1", g_pkg$note))
stopifnot(!anyNA(g_width), g_width[3] < min(g_width[1:2]),
          max(g_art$value[1:2] - g_pkg$value[1:2]) < 0.01)
```

The interval for the Gini index is the procedure of Chattopadhyay and De
(2016). Their simulation study draws from three populations: a gamma
distribution with shape 2.649 and rate 0.84, a lognormal distribution with
log mean 2.185 and log standard deviation 0.562, and a Pareto distribution
with scale 20,000 and shape 5. For each, the study computed the Gini index
and the asymptotic variance of its estimator (the article's Equation 6) by
numerical integration, with no package code. The table compares those
population values with the mean of `gini_index()` and the mean of the
variance estimate that `seq_aipe_gini()` reports, over
`r int(g_pop$replications[1])` samples of 2,000 observations.

```{r gini-table}
long_table(g_pop, digits = 4, reference = "Population value")
```

The largest difference is `r largest(g_pop)` standard errors: the package
estimates the quantities the article defines. The population variances can
themselves be checked against the posted version of the article discussed
next, whose table prints the optimal fixed sample size for a half width of
0.01 at 90%: these variances give `r listing(int(g_fixed))` for the three
populations, and the table prints 1,267, 1,424, and 686.

The sequential procedure itself is compared with the simulation table of the
version of the article that its authors posted in 2015 (Chattopadhyay & De,
2015, Table 1, p. 19): 2,000 studies for each population of a 90% interval
with a half width of 0.01, which is a full width of 0.02 in the package's
terms, starting from a pilot sample of
`r ceiling(2 * qnorm(0.95) / 0.02)`. The rows were run through
`seq_aipe_gini_pilot()` and `seq_aipe_gini()`.

```{r gini-procedure-table}
g_show <- g_sim
g_show$condition <- sub(";.*$", "", g_sim$condition)
g_show$quantity <- sub(" \\(the estimate plus and minus 0.01\\)", "", g_sim$quantity)
long_table(g_show, digits = ifelse(grepl("coverage", g_sim$quantity), 4, 1),
           reference = "Posted version", first_label = "Population")
```

The article's interval is the estimate plus and minus the half width, 0.01.
`seq_aipe_gini()` reports a different interval, the estimate plus and minus z
times its estimated standard error, as the package's other procedures do.
When the rule is met that interval is never wider than the target, and the
smaller the sample in which the rule is met, the narrower it is. The table
therefore counts coverage twice in the same studies: for the article's
interval (the `gini` row plus and minus 0.01), which is what compares with
the posted table, and for the interval the package reports.

*Final sample size.* The lognormal and Pareto rows are reproduced
(`r num(log_n$z, 1)` and `r num(par_n$z, 1)` standard errors). The gamma row
is not. The package's mean final sample size is `r num(gam_n$value, 1)`
against `r num(gam_n$published, 1)`,
`r num(100 * (gam_n$value / gam_n$published - 1), 1)` percent higher and
`r num(gam_n$z, 1)` standard errors away, and its standard deviation is
`r num(sd_here(gam_n), 0)` where the posted standard error implies
`r num(sd_published(gam_n, 2000), 0)` (for the lognormal population the two
are `r num(sd_here(log_n), 0)` and `r num(sd_published(log_n, 2000), 0)`, and
for the Pareto population `r num(sd_here(par_n), 0)` and
`r num(sd_published(par_n, 2000), 0)`). The largest final sample sizes are
similar (`r int(gam_range[2])` here and `r int(gam_range[3])` in the posted
version), which suggests that the posted gamma studies include final sample
sizes well below the smallest found here (`r int(gam_range[1])`). The cause
cannot be settled without the code behind the posted table.

*Coverage.* The article's interval covers `r listing(num(g_art$value, 4))` of
the time for the gamma, lognormal, and Pareto populations against the posted
`r listing(sub("0$", "", num(g_art$published, 4)))`
(`r listing(num(g_art$z, 1))` standard errors). The interval the package
reports covers `r listing(num(g_pkg$value, 4))`.
For the gamma and lognormal populations the two intervals hardly differ: the
package's has a mean width of `r num(g_width[1], 4)` and
`r num(g_width[2], 4)` where the article's is 0.02. For the Pareto
population, where the rule is met in smaller samples
(`r num(par_n$value, 0)` observations on average), its mean width is
`r num(g_width[3], 4)`, and it covers
`r num(100 * (g_art$value[3] - g_pkg$value[3]), 1)` percentage points less
often than the article's interval in the same studies. The coverage of the
procedure at wide targets is in the last section.

## Two Stage Procedures With Exact Properties

```{r classical}
cl_all <- rows("classical")
cl <- cl_all[cl_all$kind == "exact calculation", ]
cl2 <- cl_all[cl_all$kind == "exact calculation, second run", ]
flagged <- cl[abs(cl$z) > 3, ]
stopifnot(nrow(cl) + nrow(cl2) == nrow(cl_all))
# What the second runs showed, in words.
second_text <- if (nrow(flagged) == 0L) {
  "No value was more than three standard errors from its exact value, so no second run was needed."
} else {
  pieces <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(flagged)), function(i) {
    f <- flagged[i, ]
    g <- cl2[cl2$procedure == f$procedure & cl2$condition == f$condition &
               cl2$quantity == f$quantity, ]
    stopifnot(nrow(g) == 1L)
    sprintf("the %s of `%s` (%s) was %s in the first %s studies, %s standard errors %s the exact %s, and %s in the second %s (z = %s)",
            f$quantity, f$procedure, sub("^.*; ", "", f$condition), num(f$value, 4),
            int(f$replications), num(abs(f$z), 1), if (f$z < 0) "below" else "above",
            num(f$published, 4), num(g$value, 4), int(g$replications), num(g$z, 1))
  }, character(1))
  second_of_flagged <- cl2[paste(cl2$procedure, cl2$condition, cl2$quantity) %in%
                             paste(flagged$procedure, flagged$condition, flagged$quantity), ]
  paste0("Under the rule described at the top of the page, a condition with a value more than three standard errors from its exact value was run a second time. That happened ",
         if (nrow(flagged) == 1L) "once: " else paste0(nrow(flagged), " times: "),
         paste(pieces, collapse = "; "), ". ",
         if (all(abs(second_of_flagged$z) <= 3))
           "The second run agrees with the exact value, so the first difference was chance."
         else "The second run does not agree with the exact value either, which points to a defect.")
}
cov_rows <- cl[cl$quantity == "coverage", ]
risk_rows <- cl[cl$quantity == "risk relative to the bound", ]
worst <- one("classical", condition = "n* = 44", quantity = "risk relative to the bound")
```

Four of the two stage procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) have
properties that hold exactly, not only in large samples: Stein's (1945)
interval for a normal mean (`ts_fwd_norm_mean()`), the interval for the
location of a negative exponential distribution (`ts_fwd_nexp_mean()`), and
the bounded risk procedures for a normal mean (`ts_br_norm_mean()`) and an
exponential mean (`ts_br_exp_mean()`; the book's Section 8.3.2, Equation
8.3.13). In each the total sample size depends on the first stage through one
statistic whose distribution is known, so the expected sample size and the
coverage or the risk can be computed exactly. The study does that calculation
in base R, with no package code, and compares it with what the package's
functions did in simulated studies: a first stage, the total sample size the
function asks for, a second stage of that size, and the final interval or
estimate.

```{r classical-table}
cl_show <- cl_all
cl_show$condition <- paste0("`", cl_all$procedure, "` ", cl_all$condition,
                            ifelse(cl_all$kind == "exact calculation", "", " (second run)"))
long_table(cl_show, digits = ifelse(cl_all$quantity == "mean total sample size", 2, 4),
           reference = "Exact")
```

Of the `r nrow(cl)` simulated values of the first runs, `r within(cl)` are
within two standard errors of the exact ones and `r within(cl, 3)` within
three. `r second_text` The exact values themselves show the guarantees: coverage
is at least 0.95 in every interval row (from
`r num(min(cov_rows$published), 4)` to `r num(max(cov_rows$published), 4)`),
and the risk is at most the bound in every bounded risk row (from
`r num(min(risk_rows$published), 3)` to `r num(max(risk_rows$published), 3)`
of it). The row with n\* = 44 and a first stage of 14 was chosen because it
is where `ts_br_exp_mean()` comes closest to its bound: its help page
reports an exact calculation over first stages of 3 to 100 and values of
n\* up to 2,000 in which the risk never exceeded the bound and was largest,
0.990 of it, for a first stage of 14 or 15 with n\* near 44. The exact risk
in that row is `r num(worst$published, 4)` of the bound. For this procedure
the bound rests on computation of that kind and not on a theorem, as the
help page explains.

The other classical procedures (the purely sequential procedures for a mean,
the purely sequential interval for a median, and the distribution free two
stage interval) have asymptotic guarantees only. No published table is
compared for them here; the last section measures them at wide targets.

## Where the Package Departs From an Article

In several places the package does something other than what a source
article prints. This section gives the evidence for four of them, each
deliberate and documented in the help page of the function concerned. Three
more are described elsewhere: the interval that `seq_aipe_gini()` reports,
which is not the interval of its source article (the section on the Gini
index above and the last section), the default allocation rule of the budget
procedure (the section on the budget above and the help page of
`seq_budget()`), and the power to which one factor is raised in the two cost
sample sizes of the 2017 article (the help page of `seq_mr_smd()`).

### A Variance Estimate That Is Zero or Negative

```{r dep-unusable}
du <- rows("departures", source = "Table 2")
du_printed <- du[du$kind == "rule as printed", ]
du_package <- du[du$kind == "deliberate departure", ]
early <- sub("^.*in ([0-9.]+)% of studies$", "\\1", du_printed$note[1])
```

The estimate of the asymptotic variance on which a stopping rule rests can be
zero or negative in a small sample. The articles replace it with a small
positive number, n<sup>-3</sup>, and evaluate the rule, under which a study
can stop at once with an interval far narrower than its data support. The
package reports such a check as not met, so sampling continues (a positive
estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe). The study
followed the same `r int(du_printed$replications[1])` simulated studies under
both rules for the Pearson correlation at &rho; = 0.5 and a width of 0.2,
taking the rule as printed from the flag that `seq_aipe_r()` sets when the
variance estimate is unusable.

```{r dep-unusable-table}
du_show <- du
du_show$condition <- ifelse(du$kind == "rule as printed", "Rule as printed", "Package")
interval_table(du_show, label = "Rule", who = "simulated")
```

Under the rule as printed, `r early` percent of the studies stopped on an
unusable variance estimate. With those stops the rule as printed gives the
article's row (mean final sample size at
`r num(du_printed$z[du_printed$quantity == "mean final sample size"], 1)`
standard errors, coverage at
`r num(du_printed$z[du_printed$quantity == "coverage"], 1)`, mean width at
`r num(du_printed$z[du_printed$quantity == "mean interval width"], 1)`);
without them the package's studies are a little longer, cover a little more
often (`r num(du_package$value[du_package$quantity == "coverage"], 3)` against
`r num(du_printed$value[du_printed$quantity == "coverage"], 3)`), and end
with intervals that are wider on average
(`r num(du_package$value[du_package$quantity == "mean interval width"], 4)`
against
`r num(du_printed$value[du_printed$quantity == "mean interval width"], 4)`),
because the intervals of the early stops were far narrower than the target.

### The Variance of the Coefficient of Variation

```{r dep-cv}
dc <- rows("departures", condition = "coefficient of variation 0.8")
mse30 <- one("departures", kind = "sampling variance", source = "Equation 30",
             condition = "coefficient of variation 0.8")
mse9 <- one("departures", kind = "sampling variance", source = "Equation 9",
            condition = "coefficient of variation 0.8")
dep16 <- rows("mrpe_cv_2016", kind = "deliberate departure")
dn <- dep16[dep16$quantity == "mean final sample size", ]
dopt <- dep16[dep16$quantity == "optimal sample size with known parameters", ]
pn <- pub16[match(dn$condition, pub16$condition), ]
eff <- function(x) as.numeric(sub("^risk efficiency ([0-9.]+).*$", "\\1", x$note))
normal_rows <- grepl("^normal", dn$condition)
gamma_rows <- grepl("^gamma", dn$condition)
lognormal_rows <- grepl("^lognormal", dn$condition)
stopifnot(sum(lognormal_rows) == 1L)
```

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, Equation 9, p. 631) and Kelley, Darku, and
Chattopadhyay (2018, Equation 30, p. 233) give different expressions for the
asymptotic variance of the sample coefficient of variation. The 2018
expression minus the 2016 one is
(kurtosis &minus; 3) &kappa;<sup>2</sup> (1 &minus; &kappa;<sup>2</sup>) / 4,
where &kappa; is the coefficient of variation: the two agree when the
kurtosis of the population is 3, as it is for a normal population (and when
&kappa; is exactly 1), and differ otherwise. For a gamma population with a
coefficient of variation of 0.8 the two expressions give
`r num(mse9$published, 4)` and `r num(mse30$published, 4)`. Simulation
settles which describes the estimator: n times its mean squared error in
samples of 2,000 was `r num(mse30$value, 4)` (standard error
`r num(mse30$se, 4)`).

```{r dep-cv-table}
dc_show <- dc
dc_show$condition <- sub("^Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay \\(2018\\), |^Chattopadhyay and Kelley \\(2016\\), ",
                         "", dc$source)
dc_show$quantity <- sprintf("%s; %s", dc$procedure, sub("^.*; ", "", dc$condition))
long_table(dc_show, digits = 4, reference = "Formula", first_label = "Compared with",
           quantity_label = "Estimate", value_label = "Estimate (SE)")
```

The simulated value agrees with Equation 30 of the 2018 article and is
`r num(mse9$z, 0)` standard errors from Equation 9 of the 2016 article. The
default of `seq_mr_cv()` therefore estimates the 2018 expression, and
`variance = "published"` estimates the 2016 one, as the last two rows of the
table confirm. The choice changes the sample size at which the procedure
stops:

```{r dep-cv-n}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  sub("; A = .*$", "", dn$condition),
  num(pn$published, 1), num(dopt$published, 0), num(ceiling(dopt$value), 0),
  num(pn$value, 1), num(dn$value, 1), num(eff(pn), 3), num(eff(dn), 3)),
  align = c("l", rep("r", 7)),
  col.names = c("Population", "Mean N, article", "Optimal n, article", "Optimal n, package",
                "Mean N, published variance", "Mean N, default variance",
                "Risk efficiency, published", "Risk efficiency, default"))
```

"Optimal n" is the sample size that minimizes the risk when the population
is known: the article computes it from its Equation 9 and the package from
Equation 30, rounded up. For the normal populations the two agree and so do
the two procedures, within
`r num(max(abs(dn$value[normal_rows] / pn$value[normal_rows] - 1)) * 100, 1)`
percent in mean final sample size. For the gamma and lognormal populations
the article's optimal sample size is too small, and its procedure stops
early: at a coefficient of variation of 0.8 the published variance stops at a
mean of `r num(pn$value[grepl("gamma, coefficient of variation 0.8", pn$condition)], 0)`
observations and the default at
`r num(dn$value[grepl("gamma, coefficient of variation 0.8", dn$condition)], 0)`,
where the risk is smallest near
`r num(ceiling(dopt$value[grepl("gamma, coefficient of variation 0.8", dopt$condition)]), 0)`.
Risk efficiency is the realized risk divided by the smallest attainable risk
(standard errors of about `r num(mean(as.numeric(sub("^.*standard error ([0-9.]+).*$", "\\1", dn$note))), 3)`).
The risk is flat near its minimum, so stopping early costs less than the
sample sizes suggest: with the published variance the risk efficiency is
`r num(min(eff(pn)[gamma_rows]), 2)` to `r num(max(eff(pn)[gamma_rows]), 2)` for
the gamma populations and `r num(eff(pn)[lognormal_rows], 2)` for the lognormal
one, against `r num(min(eff(dn)[!normal_rows]), 2)` to
`r num(max(eff(dn)[!normal_rows]), 2)` with the default. The option exists so
that the article's results, and those of `DMAR::mr_cv()`, which implements the
article's rule, can be reproduced.

### Equation 26 of the 2018 Article

```{r dep-eq26}
d26 <- rows("departures", condition = "skewed in opposite directions")
v26c <- one("departures", kind = "sampling variance", source = "as corrected",
            condition = "skewed in opposite directions")
v26p <- one("departures", kind = "sampling variance", source = "as printed",
            condition = "skewed in opposite directions")
e26c <- one("departures", kind = "estimator", source = "as corrected",
            condition = "skewed in opposite directions")
```

Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, p. 232), the
asymptotic variance of the standardized mean difference, omits a factor of
one half in its second term. The authors' correction is posted at
<https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf>
and ships with the package (`system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package =
"SMSD")`). The two forms differ only when the groups differ in mean and in
skewness. For two populations with unit variance, a standardized mean
difference of 0.5, and skewness in opposite directions (a standardized chi
square with 3 degrees of freedom and its mirror image), the corrected form
gives `r num(v26c$published, 4)` and the printed form
`r num(v26p$published, 4)`.

```{r dep-eq26-table}
d26_show <- d26
d26_show$condition <- sub("^Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay \\(2018\\), ", "", d26$source)
d26_show$quantity <- sprintf("%s; %s", d26$procedure, sub("^.*; ", "", d26$condition))
long_table(d26_show, digits = 4, reference = "Formula", first_label = "Compared with",
           quantity_label = "Estimate", value_label = "Estimate (SE)")
```

In samples of 1,000 per group, n times the variance of the sample
standardized mean difference was `r num(v26c$value, 3)` (standard error
`r num(v26c$se, 3)`), which is `r num(v26c$z, 1)` standard errors from the
corrected value and `r num(v26p$z, 0)` from the printed one. The variance
estimate of `seq_aipe_smd()` averaged `r num(e26c$value, 4)`: it estimates
the corrected form.

### The Stopping Rule for the Squared Multiple Correlation

```{r dep-r2}
dr <- rows("departures", condition = "2 predictors, population value 0.9")
dr13 <- dr[grepl("Table 13", dr$source) & dr$quantity == "mean final sample size", ]
dr14 <- dr[grepl("Table 14", dr$source) & dr$quantity == "mean final sample size", ]
pk13 <- one("r2_2019", source = "Table 13", condition = "2 predictors, population value 0.9",
            quantity = "mean final sample size")
pk14 <- one("r2_2019", source = "Table 14", condition = "2 predictors, population value 0.9",
            quantity = "mean final sample size")
```

For the Wald interval the article's Equation 63 (p. 505), as printed, stops
at the first n that is at least
(16 z<sup>2</sup> / w<sup>2</sup>) (R<sup>2</sup> + 1/n) (1 &minus; (R<sup>2</sup> + 1/n))<sup>2</sup>,
where w is the target width and z the normal quantile for the confidence level. `seq_aipe_R2()` uses
(R<sup>2</sup> + 1/n) (1 &minus; R<sup>2</sup> + 1/n)<sup>2</sup> in its place:
the correction 1/n is added inside the second factor, where the printed form
subtracts it. The two forms differ most when the population value is large.
The study evaluated the printed form on the estimates that `seq_aipe_R2()`
reports at each stage, for the two rows with 2 predictors and a population
value of 0.9:

```{r dep-r2-table}
dr_show <- dr
dr_show$condition <- sprintf("%s, %s", sub("^.*(Table [0-9]+).*$", "\\1", dr$source),
                             sub("^.*, ", "", dr$condition))
interval_table(dr_show, n_digits = 2, label = "Equation 63 as printed", who = "simulated")
```

The printed form gives mean final sample sizes of `r num(dr13$value, 2)` and
`r num(dr14$value, 2)`, which are `r num(abs(dr13$z), 0)` and
`r num(abs(dr14$z), 0)` standard errors below the article's
`r num(dr13$published, 2)` and `r num(dr14$published, 2)` and barely above
the pilot sample sizes of `r ceiling(4 * qnorm(0.95) / 0.10)` and
`r ceiling(4 * qnorm(0.975) / 0.10)`. The form the package uses gives
`r num(pk13$value, 2)` and `r num(pk14$value, 2)` for the same rows
(`r num(pk13$z, 1)` and `r num(pk14$z, 1)` standard errors from the
article), and reproduces the other Wald rows shown earlier. The package
therefore implements the form that the article's tables were evidently
computed with, and its help page says so.

## What the Procedures Do Not Guarantee at Wide Targets

```{r wide}
wide_all <- rows("wide_targets")
shown_order <- c("seq_aipe_smd()", "seq_aipe_sm()", "seq_aipe_c()", "seq_aipe_r(), Pearson",
                 "seq_aipe_r(), Kendall", "seq_aipe_r(), Spearman", "seq_aipe_reg_coef()",
                 "seq_aipe_cv()", "seq_aipe_gini()", "seq_aipe_R2(), Wald interval",
                 "ts_fwd_dfr_mean()")
classical_order <- c("seq_fwd_norm_mean()", "seq_fwd_dfr_mean()", "seq_fwd_nexp_mean()",
                     "seq_blci_dfr_median()", "seq_br_norm_mean()", "seq_mr_norm_mean()",
                     "seq_mr_exp_mean()")
gini_both <- "seq_aipe_gini_pilot(), seq_aipe_gini()"
stopifnot(all(wide_all$procedure %in% c(shown_order, classical_order, gini_both)))
# The Gini index with two intervals in the same studies.
gi <- wide_all[wide_all$procedure == gini_both, ]
gi_at <- function(width, quantity) {
  x <- gi[grepl(paste0("width ", width, "$"), gi$condition) &
            grepl(quantity, gi$quantity, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one row for the Gini index at width ", width, call. = FALSE)
  x
}
gi_width <- function(width) sub("^mean width ", "", gi_at(width, "the package reports")$note)
wd <- wide_all[wide_all$kind == "nominal level" & wide_all$procedure %in% shown_order, ]
wd <- wd[order(match(wd$procedure, shown_order)), ]
# The purely sequential classical procedures: coverage rows and risk rows.
cs <- wide_all[wide_all$procedure %in% classical_order, ]
cs <- cs[order(match(cs$procedure, classical_order)), ]
cs_at <- function(procedure, condition) {
  x <- cs[cs$procedure == procedure & grepl(condition, cs$condition, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one row for: ", procedure, " ", condition, call. = FALSE)
  x
}
wide_at <- function(condition, procedure = NULL) {
  x <- wd[wd$condition == condition, ]
  if (!is.null(procedure)) x <- x[grepl(procedure, x$procedure, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one row for: ", condition, call. = FALSE)
  x
}
cv_of <- function(condition, procedure = NULL) wide_at(condition, procedure)$value
n_of <- function(condition, procedure = NULL) wide_at(condition, procedure)$mean_n
dfr_at <- function(population) sprintf("%s, standard deviation 2; half width 0.2, first stage of 30",
                                       population)
r2_at <- function(p, width) sprintf("squared multiple correlation 0.5, %d predictors; width %g",
                                    p, width)
holds <- wd[grepl("seq_aipe_smd|seq_aipe_sm\\(|seq_aipe_c\\(", wd$procedure), ]
low_hold <- holds[which.min(holds$value), ]
stopifnot(low_hold$procedure == "seq_aipe_c()")
dfr_exact <- rows("wide_targets", kind = "exact calculation")
```

The sequential intervals for effect sizes deliver the requested width by
construction: the final interval is never wider than the target. Their
coverage is a different kind of property. The articles prove that it
approaches the confidence level as the target width shrinks, that is, as the
sample the rule asks for grows. They do not prove, and it is not true, that
coverage is close to the confidence level at every width. When the rule is
met in a small sample, coverage can be far below nominal.

The table gives the coverage of 95% intervals measured in this study, with
the default pilot sample size unless the row says otherwise, and the mean
final sample size (per group for the standardized mean difference and the
contrast, pairs for the correlations and the slope). "Skewed" data are
standardized chi square variables with 3 degrees of freedom. The help pages
of the functions report separate runs of some of these designs, often
rounded to two decimals. A figure there can differ from the one here by up
to about 0.02, several times the standard errors shown here, because each
run has its own Monte Carlo error and some of those runs are smaller than
these.

```{r wide-table}
wd_show <- wd
wd_show$condition <- paste0("`", wd$procedure, "` ", wd$condition)
knitr::kable(data.frame(wd_show$condition, num(wd$mean_n, 1), with_se(wd$value, wd$se, 3),
                        int(wd$replications), wd$note),
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
             col.names = c("Procedure and condition", "Mean N", "Coverage (SE)",
                           "Replications", "Note"))
```

What the table shows, stated plainly:

- **Where the shortfall is small.** For the standardized mean difference, the
  standardized mean, and the contrast, coverage is between
  `r num(min(holds$value), 3)` and `r num(max(holds$value), 3)` in the
  `r nrow(holds)` conditions above. The lowest is the contrast at a width of
  `r sub("^.*; width ", "", low_hold$condition)`, which stops with about
  `r num(low_hold$mean_n, 0)` observations per group.
- **The Pearson correlation.** At a correlation of 0.4 coverage is
  `r num(cv_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.4"), 2)` at a width of 0.4 and
  `r num(cv_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.2"), 2)` at 0.2. A stronger
  correlation is estimated with less sampling error, so the rule is met
  sooner and coverage is worse at the same width:
  `r num(cv_of("correlation 0.8, normal; width 0.4"), 2)` and
  `r num(cv_of("correlation 0.8, normal; width 0.2"), 2)` at 0.8, and
  `r num(cv_of("correlation 0.9, normal; width 0.1"), 2)` at a correlation of
  0.9 with a width of 0.1. Skewed data lower it further
  (`r num(cv_of("correlation 0.4, skewed; width 0.4"), 2)` at 0.4 and a
  width of 0.4).
- **The regression slope** behaves like the correlation:
  `r num(cv_of("slope 0.5, normal; width 0.4"), 2)` for a slope of 0.5 at a
  width of 0.4, `r num(cv_of("slope 0.5, skewed; width 0.4"), 2)` with skewed
  data, and `r num(cv_of("slope 2, normal; width 0.2"), 2)` for a slope of 2
  at a width of 0.2.
- **The rank correlations** fall short at a strong association too:
  `r num(cv_of("bivariate normal, rho = 0.8; width 0.4", "Kendall"), 2)`
  (Kendall) and
  `r num(cv_of("bivariate normal, rho = 0.8; width 0.4", "Spearman"), 2)`
  (Spearman) at &rho; = 0.8 and a width of 0.4.
- **The coefficient of variation** is sensitive to skewness. At a value of
  0.5 coverage is `r num(cv_of("coefficient of variation 0.5, gamma; width 0.2"), 2)`
  for gamma data and
  `r num(cv_of("coefficient of variation 0.5, lognormal; width 0.2"), 2)` for
  lognormal data at a width of 0.2, and still
  `r num(cv_of("coefficient of variation 0.5, lognormal; width 0.1"), 2)` for
  lognormal data at 0.1, with a mean of
  `r num(n_of("coefficient of variation 0.5, lognormal; width 0.1"), 0)`
  observations.
- **The Gini index** covers
  `r num(cv_of("Gini index 0.3, lognormal; width 0.2"), 2)` and
  `r num(cv_of("Gini index 0.3, lognormal; width 0.1"), 2)` of the time at
  widths of 0.2 and 0.1. That is the interval `seq_aipe_gini()` reports,
  which is not the interval of Chattopadhyay and De (2016); the two are set
  side by side below.
- **The squared multiple correlation** fails badly when the number of
  predictors is not small beside the sample size the width calls for:
  for a population value of 0.5 at a width of 0.3 coverage is
  `r num(cv_of(r2_at(5, 0.3)), 2)` with 5 predictors,
  `r num(cv_of(r2_at(10, 0.3)), 2)` with 10, and
  `r num(cv_of(r2_at(15, 0.3)), 2)` with 15, and at a width of 0.2 it is
  `r num(cv_of(r2_at(10, 0.2)), 2)` with 10.
  The procedure also assumes multivariate normal data.
- **The distribution free two stage interval for a mean**
  (`ts_fwd_dfr_mean()`) plugs the first stage variance into the known
  variance sample size with no allowance for having estimated it. With a first
  stage of 30 its coverage for a narrow target is
  `r num(cv_of(dfr_at("normal")), 3)` for normal data (the exact value is
  `r num(dfr_exact$published[grepl("half width 0.2", dfr_exact$condition)], 3)`),
  `r num(cv_of(dfr_at("exponential (skewness 2)")), 3)` for exponential data,
  and `r num(cv_of(dfr_at("lognormal (skewness 4)")), 3)` for lognormal data
  with a skewness of 4. Narrowing the target does not remove the shortfall
  while the first stage stays at 30; a larger first stage reduces it.

### The Gini Index: Two Intervals

```{r wide-gini}
stopifnot(nrow(gi) == 4L,
          gi_at("0.2", "the article's")$value > 0.95, gi_at("0.1", "the article's")$value > 0.95,
          gi_at("0.2", "the package reports")$value < 0.95,
          gi_at("0.1", "the package reports")$value < 0.95)
```

The interval of Chattopadhyay and De (2016) is the estimate plus and minus
half the target width. `seq_aipe_gini()` reports the estimate plus and minus z
times its estimated standard error, which the stopping rule keeps below the
target, and well below it when the rule is met in a small sample. The study
ran the two wide conditions above again through `seq_aipe_gini_pilot()` and
`seq_aipe_gini()`, with new data, and counted the coverage of both intervals
in the same studies.

```{r wide-gini-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(sub("^Gini index 0.3, ", "", gi$condition),
                        sub(" \\(the estimate plus and minus half the width\\)", "", gi$quantity),
                        num(gi$mean_n, 1), with_se(gi$value, gi$se, 3), int(gi$replications),
                        ifelse(grepl("^mean width", gi$note), gi$note, "")),
             align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
             col.names = c("Condition", "Quantity", "Mean N", "Coverage (SE)", "Replications",
                           "Note"))
```

At a target width of 0.2 the interval the package reports has a mean width
of `r gi_width("0.2")` and covers
`r num(gi_at("0.2", "the package reports")$value, 3)` of the time; the
article's interval covers `r num(gi_at("0.2", "the article's")$value, 3)` in
the same studies. At 0.1 the two figures are
`r num(gi_at("0.1", "the package reports")$value, 3)` (mean width
`r gi_width("0.1")`) and `r num(gi_at("0.1", "the article's")$value, 3)`. At
these targets the shortfall belongs to the interval the package reports and
not to the article's procedure, whose interval covers more often than its
nominal level here. The article's interval can be formed from the package's
output: it is the `gini` row plus and minus half of `width`, once the rule is
met.

### The Purely Sequential Classical Procedures

```{r wide-classical}
fn_wide <- cs_at("seq_fwd_norm_mean()", "half width 0.77")
fn_narrow <- cs_at("seq_fwd_norm_mean()", "half width 0.25")
fd_norm <- cs_at("seq_fwd_dfr_mean()", "normal")
fd_exp <- cs_at("seq_fwd_dfr_mean()", "exponential, standard deviation 2; half width 0.5")
fd_exp_narrow <- cs_at("seq_fwd_dfr_mean()", "exponential, standard deviation 2; half width 0.25")
fx <- cs_at("seq_fwd_nexp_mean()", "width 0.24")
med <- cs[cs$procedure == "seq_blci_dfr_median()", ]
br2 <- cs_at("seq_br_norm_mean()", "squared error")
br1 <- cs_at("seq_br_norm_mean()", "absolute error")
mrn <- cs_at("seq_mr_norm_mean()", "normal")
mre <- cs_at("seq_mr_exp_mean()", "exponential")
n_star <- function(x) sub("^.*\\(n\\* = ([0-9,]+)\\)$", "\\1", x$condition)
stopifnot(nrow(med) == 3L)
```

The purely sequential procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) check
their rule after every observation. Their confidence level, their risk bound,
or their optimality holds in the limit as the target narrows, and none of
them has a `*_sensitivity()` function, so the study ran each through its
pilot function and its check function, with the default pilot, at a target
near the least favorable one that its help page reports. In the table n\* is
the sample size that would be needed if the population were known. For an
interval the target is the nominal 0.95. For the bounded risk procedure it is
a risk of at most 1 times the bound, and for the minimum risk procedures it
is a risk close to 1 times the smallest attainable.

```{r wide-classical-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(paste0("`", cs$procedure, "` ", cs$condition), cs$quantity,
                        num(cs$mean_n, 1), with_se(cs$value, cs$se, 3), int(cs$replications)),
             align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Procedure and condition", "Quantity", "Mean N", "Value (SE)",
                           "Replications"))
```

- **The fixed width interval for a normal mean** (`seq_fwd_norm_mean()`)
  covers `r num(fn_wide$value, 3)` of the time when about `r n_star(fn_wide)`
  observations are needed and `r num(fn_narrow$value, 3)` when about
  `r n_star(fn_narrow)` are. Stein's two stage interval, `ts_fwd_norm_mean()`,
  is the alternative whose level is guaranteed.
- **The distribution free interval for a mean** (`seq_fwd_dfr_mean()`) covers
  `r num(fd_norm$value, 3)` for normal data when about `r n_star(fd_norm)`
  observations are needed. For exponential data with the same standard
  deviation it covers `r num(fd_exp$value, 3)` at that target and
  `r num(fd_exp_narrow$value, 3)` when about `r n_star(fd_exp_narrow)` are
  needed: skewness slows the approach to the stated level considerably.
- **The interval for the location of a negative exponential distribution**
  (`seq_fwd_nexp_mean()`) covers `r num(fx$value, 3)` when about
  `r n_star(fx)` observations are needed. Here too the two stage interval,
  `ts_fwd_nexp_mean()`, has a guaranteed level.
- **The interval for a median** (`seq_blci_dfr_median()`) has at least its
  stated coverage at any fixed sample size, but the sequential procedure stops
  when the interval happens to be short. Its coverage is
  `r num(min(med$value), 3)` to `r num(max(med$value), 3)` in the
  `r count_word(nrow(med))` conditions above, and the shortfall does not go
  away quickly: it is `r num(med$value[which.max(med$mean_n)], 3)` in the
  condition that ends with about `r num(max(med$mean_n), 0)` observations.
- **The bounded risk procedure for a normal mean** (`seq_br_norm_mean()`)
  approaches its bound from above. When the bound calls for about
  `r n_star(br2)` observations under squared error loss the risk is
  `r num(br2$value, 2)` times the bound, and when it calls for about
  `r n_star(br1)` under absolute error loss it is `r num(br1$value, 2)` times
  the bound. The two stage procedure `ts_br_norm_mean()` keeps its risk at
  or below the bound for normal data, as the exact results above show.
- **The minimum risk procedures** attain the smallest risk only in the limit:
  the risk of `seq_mr_norm_mean()` is `r num(mrn$value, 2)` times the smallest
  attainable when the best sample size is `r n_star(mrn)`, and that of
  `seq_mr_exp_mean()` is `r num(mre$value, 2)` times when it is
  `r n_star(mre)`. (`seq_mr_nexp_mean()` and `seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()` are not in
  the study; their help pages report the same kind of figures.)

### What Helps

A larger pilot sample helps where the shortfall comes from stopping early. A
minimum pilot sample size of 40 raised coverage from
`r num(cv_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.4"), 2)` to
`r num(cv_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.4, m_0 = 40"), 2)` for the
correlation of 0.4 at a width of 0.4, and from
`r num(cv_of("slope 0.5, normal; width 0.4"), 2)` to
`r num(cv_of("slope 0.5, normal; width 0.4, m_0 = 40"), 2)` for the slope of
0.5, at a cost of
`r num(n_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.4, m_0 = 40") - n_of("correlation 0.4, normal; width 0.4"), 0)`
and
`r num(n_of("slope 0.5, normal; width 0.4, m_0 = 40") - n_of("slope 0.5, normal; width 0.4"), 0)`
more pairs on average. It is not a cure for a strong relationship or for
skewed data.

The practical rule follows from the tables. Before relying on an interval at
a planned width, run the matching `*_sensitivity()` function at each true
value that is plausible for the study, the strongest included, with data as
skewed as the study's are likely to be, and read its `coverage` row. If
coverage is low, plan a narrower width, a larger minimum pilot sample size,
or both. For a classical procedure, which has no such function, the help
page gives its measured coverage or risk over a range of targets, and where a
two stage procedure with an exact guarantee exists it is named there.

## Reproducing This Article

The study is one script. From the root of the package's repository, with
the package's source loaded or the package installed:

```r
Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE); source("data-raw/validation_study.R")'
```

It writes `data-raw/validation_results.rds`, a data frame with one row per
comparison (the procedure, the source with its table and page, the
condition, the published value and its standard error, the package's value
and its standard error, the number of replications, and z), with the seed,
the date, and the package version as attributes. The replication counts are
in the tables above; the cached file was made on `r attr(res, "date")` with
SMSD `r attr(res, "package_version")` under `r attr(res, "r_version")`. Every
part of every condition sets its own seed, so a second run of the script
gives the same numbers. The script uses 6 cores unless the environment
variable `SMSD_VALIDATION_CORES` says otherwise. On Windows, where R cannot
run the parts as forked processes, it uses one core and takes several hours.
The script's header describes settings for a shorter trial run or for some
conditions only; this article refuses a cache made that way.
